utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you. May I have appearances for counsel, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honour pleases, my name is Niemann and I appear for the Prosecution. Mr. Keegan will shortly join us, and I am assisted at the bar table by Miss Sutherland, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you. May I have appearances for the defence, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Milan Vujin, lead defence counsel. Today I am assisted by Mr. Nikola Kostic, and Mr. John Livingston as a law adviser, and Ms. Jelena Lopicic is also a law adviser.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vujin. Are you ready to proceed, Mr. Vujin? Mr. Vujin, are you ready to proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Defence believed that we would follow the order as we have been doing in the presentation of evidence, which means that the Prosecutor will present his evidence, or rather his position, and that after that the Defence would speak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, do you have any objection to proceeding in that way?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, in terms of presenting the material that we wish to present, we have presented certain material which has been served upon the Defence in relation to written submissions, in the form of written submissions and in addition to that certain supporting material, including two declarations. That is our position. We wish to make oral submissions. We ask the court for an opportunity to do that, but we don't seek to do that until after we have heard the evidence of the defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Vujin, there is outstanding a request for postponement of sentence that you filed on June 26th, and actually I wanted you to speak to that. You were asking that the sentencing be postponed. You wished to call in person an expert witness. We have received his report, and we have read his report, but you may proceed with respect to that motion, unless you wish to withdraw it at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this moment we would not like to withdraw the proposal to invite as an expert witness Professor Nedopil. However, as you have been able to see, we have had problems in communications with Professor Nedopil who was at a conference in Canada. I spoke to him on the phone today and he is ready to come to The Hague but not before Friday, because he is prevented by other obligations. In the meantime I wish to inform the court of another difficulty that has arisen. My office informed me half an hour ago that it had also contacted Professor Nedopil and that Professor Nedopil is asking payment not only of travelling expenses and accommodation but also 1,000 German marks per hour for every hour of his absence from Munich.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Does that include travel time? I suppose it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Yes, travel too from 6.00 am in the morning until he completes his sojourn in The Hague. The presentation of a psychiatrist and especially Professor Nedopil, we chose him because he had occasion to examine the personality of the accused Tadic for some time during his stay in Munich, but if you, as the Trial Chamber, are unable to accommodate this request in the name of a fair trial, we would be prepared to accept the expert testimony of an expert who is here in The Hague and who carried out some psychological examinations of the accused, Tadic, here in The Hague. I do not have his name at this moment, but I have asked Mr. Stuart to provide me with the names, and if there is such a possibility, the Defence would be ready to accept it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: How much will he or she charge per hour in guilders, I suppose?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: I am afraid I don't know that because this is the first time that I am encountering Dutch experts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: The situation with respect to Dr. Nedopil, as I understand it, he examined Mr. Tadic two and a half, three years ago, was it, when he was in custody in Germany. You have provided the Trial Chamber with a copy of the report and, as I indicated, we have read that report. I have discussed this matter with my colleagues, and we feel that the report is sufficient. There's no need for him to attend in person and read his report for us. So I don't really consider that it's necessary. When you filed your request for an extension, the Trial Chamber had previously entered an order stating that if you were able to obtain the presence of Dr. Nedopil by July 4th, then we would hear from him, because at that time you did not know when he was returning, and so you really could not give us a date, but now you are saying that he could be here on July 4th?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, on 4th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: In the Order that the Trial Chamber entered on July 12th, the Trial Chamber indicated that we preferred written statements. This is not a trial. This is a sentencing hearing and we are of course interested in receiving information that will help us in the process, but it need not be presented orally. So with the benefit of his report I don't believe there is any reason to have him here. With respect to the other psychiatrist who is here, would he be ready to testify this week? He, I gather, would have to examine Mr. Tadic at some point this week.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I really do not know, because I have not had any chance to communicate with the local expert, but from the information from Mr. Tadic, the psychologist who did the tests does not require additional time for observation of Mr. Tadic. She has her findings ready and she is able to present those findings. We just appeal to the court to enable us to get in touch with her so that we can agree on when she could present her findings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: In the Order of June 12th the Trial Chamber had indicated that we wished to receive any reports you intended on offering three days, I think is what was said in the Order, prior to the commencement of the hearing but when could you have that report to us? When could we receive it?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: I'm afraid we do not have that report in writing, because Mr. Tadic never received that report in writing, the view of the expert who tested him. If we receive the name of that lady, because Mr. Dusko Tadic does not know her name either, we could then provide you with an answer to your question, and I hope that this could be on the same day as soon as we get in touch with her.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I suppose you need then to speak with the Registry to obtain the name of the psychologist. You may do that. We will take a recess this afternoon, so you may do that at the recess and perhaps even you will be able to determine over the evening, when we adjourn tonight, whether the psychologist has a report, when the report would be available to be provided to the Trial Chamber. Then we will make a determination tomorrow as to whether we will hear this psychologist. You have listed a Professor Dr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Aleksic Zivojin is here present and he is ready to present his views on the circumstances that we explained in our motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: We have not received a report from Professor Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIC
utterances.text: No, you have not received a report from Professor Aleksic. If you feel that is necessary in writing, you can have it tomorrow, but we wanted to take advantage of Professor Aleksic for him to explain orally the situation with regard to Yugoslav criminal law provisions regarding the circumstances that are relevant for this case: Professor Aleksic is a world renowned figure and expert for criminal law and criminology. He has some 26 books to his credit and I am sure that he would be very useful to the Trial Chamber and all of us here to hear him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: The June 12th order directed the parties to provide a written report. That's why I was asking whether you had one available. When did you intend on calling him in the Order of witnesses you have listed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Professor Aleksic would come at the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Is he here in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Yes, he is in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Confer with him and determine whether he has a report and advise the Trial Chamber tomorrow afternoon when we continue, and then we will make a determination as to whether we will hear him if he does not have a report in light of our June 12th order directing a written report. Are there any other matters preliminarily, Mr. Vujin?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: I should just like to inform you, your Honours, that we have proposed the testimony of two witnesses, Radomir Slobodan and Javic Milan, but coming from Banja Luka to Belgrade they had a traffic accident and were therefore unable to come, so that in the course of these proceedings we hope to be able to submit the written statement by Mr. Javic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: You may be seated. Thank you. On May 7th the Trial Chamber rendered an Opinion and Judgment finding Dusko Tadic guilty of certain crimes charged in the indictment. This is a pre-sentencing hearing pursuant to Rule 100 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence of the Tribunal, and pursuant to that rule the Prosecutor and the Defence may submit any relevant information that may assist the Trial Chamber in determining an appropriate sentence. As I have indicated on that same day, the May 7th, the Trial Chamber directed the parties to provide the Trial Chamber with an indication of the submissions that each wished to make today, and the Defence has filed a sentencing notice listing the persons it intends to call and, Mr. Vujin, you have indicated that you would require 45 minutes to one hour for each person. The Prosecutor has filed a brief and material regarding the sentencing policies in the former Yugoslavia as well as two declarations from investigators and an affidavit from Hakija Elezovic. The Prosecution has also filed a request for leave to make an oral submission regarding the sentencing, and that has been granted. The Defence also filed a letter requesting the protection of certain witnesses, stating that they feared that they would be arrested while they were in The Hague. That request was opposed by the Prosecution. The Trial Chamber, however, granted that request, treating it as a motion, even though the precise requirements for those protective measures had not been established. Finally, as I have indicated in the Order of June 12th, the Trial Chamber directed the parties to coordinate immediately with the Victims and Witnesses Unit if assistance is needed for the transport of witnesses and decided that the parties may offer written statements or reports, as well as oral statements during the pre-sentence hearing, and directed the parties to submit written statements in lieu of oral statements whenever possible. The Trial Chamber also decided that any written statements or reports offered by the parties will be received and considered by the Trial Chamber in a manner equivalent to oral statements. The Prosecution has submitted two declarations by investigators and the affidavit that I referred to, and in those declarations there is information regarding the impact of Dusko Tadic's crimes. These impact statements shall be considered by the Trial Chamber to the extent that it will assist the Trial Chamber in determining the specific harm caused to the victims or to their families by the crimes of Dusko Tadic. Some of the claims of the victims as contained in those declarations relate to monetary and other losses, which cannot be verified with any certainty. The Trial Chamber, however, is not concerned with the monetary value of the loss, but only with the fact of loss, which, of course, varies with the victim's economic status. Now, during this hearing, the pre-sentencing hearing, the Trial Chamber will be concerned only with receiving submissions as to the character of the accused and other matters that may assist it in determining the appropriate sentence. We have had a lengthy trial and we have afforded the parties an ample opportunity to offer evidence as to the guilt or innocence of Mr. Tadic. Thus, we will not hear statements regarding culpability and we ask the parties to restrict their submission to matters of character and other submissions that bear on the sentencing process. Mr. Vujin, you have indicated that you wish the Prosecution to proceed first. The Prosecution has indicated that it has no objection to proceeding that way and has indicated that it would offer the declarations I gather of the investigators as well as the affidavit. Would you want to offer those into evidence, Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. I just want to clarify that we didn't wish to proceed with our oral submission now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Certainly yes, your Honour, we wish to tender the declarations and the affidavit into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Have those been provided to counsel for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Very good. They will be admitted if you do not have an extra copy at this time -- they have been filed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: They will be admitted and given an appropriate exhibit number. Is there anything else you have at this time by way of written statements?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Vujin, could you please at this time give me a list of the -- either a list or at least the names of the persons who you will be calling to give oral statements, and if there are any written statements that you wish to offer at this time also give me the author of those.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honours. We will be inviting Mr. Ljubomir Tadic; (redacted); Mr. Nikola Petrovic; Miss Valentina Tadic; Ms. Mira Tadic; and, as we have already said, Professor Zivojin Aleksic, as an expert witness. As far as written statements are concerned, at this point in time, if the Trial Chamber is inclined to accept it, I can submit two statements, one by witness Jovan Vukoje, and another from Mile Cavic, regarding the character of the accused, Dusko Tadic. Cavic, because of the traffic accident, as I said, was unable to come in person, and Mr. Vukoje because of other obligations. I apologise for omitting to mention that we also have invited Ms. Ljubica Metselaar to testify orally. She has been proposed before. She is listed under number 12 of our submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: How many copies of the written statements do you have?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: We have two copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Have you provided counsel for the Prosecution with a copy? Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: We have a copy for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Very good. These will be marked how, Mr. Bos? The first one, Mr. javic, will that be Defence Exhibit 1? The second statement, is that from -- is that Mr. or Ms. Jovan?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Mr. Jovan Vukoje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Is this a psychiatrist or psychologist?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. The microphone is not switched on. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Mr. Vukoje is director of the centre for social work in Prijedor. He is a graduate of history, geography and defectology.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: They will then be admitted as Defence Exhibit 1 for Mr. javic and 2 for Mr. Jovan, and a copy has been provided to the prosecution. As far as scheduling is concerned, as I am sure everyone understands, at this point we have only one courtroom and we have a number of matters that are being handled in this one courtroom. So we have reserved only the afternoons for today through Thursday from 2.30 until 5.30. If necessary, if we have not completed the submissions at that time on Thursday, we are available on Friday, July 4th, beginning at 10.00 am. At some point there will also be a need to use this courtroom for an initial appearance, and I will advise the parties whether that will be held in the afternoon and cut into our time. Hopefully it will be in the morning and so we will be able to use completely the 2.30-5.30 through Thursday and then perhaps all of Friday. Okay. If there's nothing else, Mr. Vujin, you may proceed and offer your first witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: We would like to call Mr. Ljubomir Tadic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Livingston, welcome. This is your first appearance here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you for being here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Ljubomir Tadic is coming. You have additional witnesses, Mr. Vujin, , but they are not in the building. They need to be brought here. So I have asked Mr. Bos to tell the Victims and Witnesses Unit to bring them to the building so that when Mr. Tadic completes his statement we can then proceed with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, when we spoke to the Witness and Victims Unit we thought that the Prosecutor would start and present his positions, as is customary, so we thought we would be inviting only one witness, because the Prosecutor told us that he would need two hours, so that there would not be time for more of our witnesses. That is why we are ready today only for the testimony of Mr. Ljubomir Tadic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: We will arrange to bring over whatever or whoever else is needed this afternoon. The Prosecution filed its submission and indicated in the submission that it would be in writing only and then filed a request for leave to make a statement as to the appropriate sentence, and, as I have indicated, I will hear from counsel, after though, we hear from the witnesses, either orally or from their written statements. So we will hear Mr. Tadic and another witness or another two witnesses should be brought over so we can proceed. When we complete all of the witnesses, we will hear from counsel, first from the Prosecution and then from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Very well, your Honour. In that case we would like to call (redacted) and Nikola Petrovic as the next witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Together?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I thought you suggested we hear Mr. Tadic and two more witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Ljubomir Tadic, and then who will be the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: (redacted).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: And the next witness after that?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: It will be Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Make sure we have enough witnesses to carry on until 5.30. Then please bring in Mr. Ljubomir Tadic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, would you take the oath that's in front of you, please? Mr. Ljubomir Tadic (sworn)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tadic. Mr. Vujin, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. Mr. Tadic, you are appearing before this Tribunal for the second time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: You have already testified in this case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: We would now like to discuss some of the circumstances which were not discussed when you first appeared before this Tribunal, and those are circumstances and facts linked to your family conditions and the personality and character of your brother, Dusko Tadic. Are you ready to answer questions on these matters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Before the conflict and the events which led to the war and armed conflict, where was your family living? When I say family, I am thinking of your father and mother and those living with him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My family was living in Kozarac, my late father, my mother, Dusko my brother, his wife and two children.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: How many children do your parents have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My parents have four sons, four sons.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: You said that your father was deceased?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he passed away in 1989.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: And your mother is alive. How is she?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She's in very poor health.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: The house in which your father and mother lived and your brother's family, is that house a family house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Did you all live there in your youth in that house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Can you tell me what were the relationships within the family, how you were brought up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Will you please describe the family relationships and your relations with your brothers when you were young?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, I have to say that our father was an officer. He was a strict man, but extremely honourable. He brought us up in the socialist communist spirit, which at that time, as you know, was widespread in Yugoslavia, that existed at the time. He never taught us any kind of nationalism. On the contrary, he would not allow us even to mention religion, because he was a communist by conviction, and communists are atheists and that is the spirit in which we were brought up, in the socialist spirit. We were members of the party while it existed. It all collapsed, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, let us go back for a moment to your relations with your brothers. I'm interested in your neighbours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Our neighbours were mostly Muslims. They were very good neighbours. We were good friends. We grew up together with them. I can only give you one example that I remember very well, though I was small. Our father was on duty. He was away and our mother was sick, and our closest neighbours, Salik Hanjic, that is our next-door-neighbour to the left, and his wife Mohiba took care of us because our mother was sick. Their house was small, as was ours in those days. We were there for seven or eight days. We slept there because our mother was in the hospital, but there weren't enough beds, so all of us lay down one next to the other, their son and us. There was never any distinction made between us.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Do you know a name called (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He's a year older than me. He lives four or five houses away.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Is he older than Dusko Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Was he friends with Dusko Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it's not the same generation. He's older than me but we all know him, and while Dusko was building his cafe, he was one of the group of young men and neighbours who were helping in building the cafe.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Is there any reason why Dusko was not close with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I'm a bit embarrassed to say it, but this boy was ill. Everyone called him "niho kuja". "Kuja" means a bitch, I'm afraid. It was generally known that he had intercourse with animals.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: That's enough. That's enough. I would like to hear about your relations with the other neighbours. Did families help each other where necessary and so on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I must tell you that in those days when we were boys we had a small house. The house that stands there now was built much later. Our father started to build it and all our neighbours helped us. In this small place and even when one doesn't have much money, one can build a house like this, because everyone will help.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Talking about that house, were there any disputes before your father's death linked to property rights amongst your brothers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Were there any disputes after your father's death?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, some slight differences, but it is well-known that after death the proceedings take some time, but in our case it didn't take very long. Our older brother may have been under somebody's influence, probably under the influence of his wife, because she was in a court proceedings in Croatia with her brother over some property, but we overcame that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Was that the former wife?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Sofija.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Could you tell me whether as a boy or later Dusko had a hobby?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, and I know quite well, Dusko as a little boy -- you know, all of us were talented painters. I'm also pretty talented for painting but Dusko had the greatest talent of all. Also Stojan, our oldest brother also used to paint, but Dusko was the youngest. I remember as a little boy he would often come in all muddy, you know, and he would make little figures, little sculptures of sorts. I remember when he was a biggish boy, when he was in 7th grade, I think, then his competence in painting and sculpture was fully expressed, and I remember that he made a bust of President Tito, and we kept it in the house for quite some time. It was made of clay. I mean, that's the only material they could use at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Can we show this photocopy so that all could see it? Could you please show it on the monitor?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: We will mark that as Exhibit 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Do you recognise the person in this picture?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course I do. This is our late father. I am not surprised at all he did such a good job. If he could do an identical image of Tito, why couldn't he do our father.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: This portrait that Dusko did in jail, is it quite realistic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is incredible. It is identical really. I have his picture. He sent me a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: While you were younger, what was the character of Dusko Tadic? Did he like to fight? Did he like to quarrel? Could you say something about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me tell you that Dusko was the youngest of our brothers. He was the pet in our family. You know what it's like when somebody is the youngest and he was everybody's pet. He was a quiet boy. He played with everybody. When I was a child I was fond of soccer football and I played football, but he didn't like that very much. He liked to paint, as I said, and this talent of his was expressed then and even after that he went to that kind of school.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: You said in addition to painting you also played football. Did Dusko Tadic have another hobby like bicycles, motorbikes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, football, he played a very little football. He played with us but he was not a very good player. I personally never saw him ride on a bicycle because I think he doesn't even know how to ride a bicycle.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: What about a motorbike?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think he can drive a motorbike either. I think in 1985 or something like that he received his driver's licence, passed his driver's test for driving a car but not a motorbike. I'm sure he doesn't know how to drive one.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: It is well-known that in your family you were all in karate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: When did Dusko start with karate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dusko started with karate just before he went to school to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: That's where he started doing that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Did he continue after Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, for some time. He didn't have much time for sports. Although he registered at a club in Kozarac and he led it for some time, but this was a smallish club, mostly children, girls.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Let us talk about the club a bit. I'm interested in the organisation of the club, who participated. Was it younger categories of people, older, the ethnic composition? How much do you know about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As you know, the club is a legal person, that is to say that it has to be registered and it has to have leadership, a management board. So most of the -- all the people there were local people, and you know that over 90 per cent of the population of Kozarac were Muslims. So it was only natural that most of them would be in the leadership of the club, because it was the children of people from Kozarac who were training there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: The children who were training there, were they Serbs, Muslims and Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember that I would come and hold a seminar there and help Dule a bit in the club and most of the children there, boys and girls -- there were less adults. Most of the members were children, boys and girls. As you know, in karate boys focus on techniques and so-called kati techniques. Dusko taught them that and children do not really fight. They compete in kati. So this was accentuated.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Did Dusko understand his activity in karate as an activity that would develop the spirit or rather fighting skills?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The kind of spirit that we had, because we trained with these people from Belgrade, this is Yazarau karate, Badaru. That means the path of friendship. Of over 100 styles that exist in the world, we adopted this style, and this is less dominant in Yugoslavia than Shotic and other styles that are more aggressive, and the symbol of this style is a pigeon, that is to say friendship and peace, and we liked that style, because that is how we fostered friendship, fraternity, unity, camaraderie.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tadic. I'm interested because you mentioned a few minutes ago when you were talking about your father and how he brought you up, and he was a partisan and he raised you in that spirit in the former Yugoslavia, I'm interested in the attitude of your family. When I say your family, I mean your family, you, Dusko Tadic, particularly Dusko Tadic, in relation to the Chetnik movement, towards the Chetnik movement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me tell you. I already said my father was a partisan. He was one of the people who organised the uprising in Kozarac. It is quite illogical that we could think of Chetniks, and we know that it was only by chance that our father survived the slaughter in Josici, because this is a Chetnik region. Our father was in the First Proletarian Brigade. He was heavily wounded. He was transferred to Josin near Celinsi. This is a Chetnik area. It wasn't that Chetniks were all over there. There were partisans there in part too. They had secured that hospital. When Dr. Mladen Stojanovic was killed, the well-known partisan commander, one night, over 50 partisans were killed that night, patients from that hospital. Our father was also a patient in that hospital, and he just happened to survive by chance, because he was lying behind the door and the knife with which they tried to kill him went through his cheek and he had a scar on his face and over here too. So he pretended to be dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Can we say that generally in your family and in the case of Dusko Tadic there was a revulsion towards Chetniks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, yes, of course. Perhaps people could even have problems because of that, but I am never going to wear a Chetnik symbol, and not a single person from my family would ever do that ever.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: I am asking you this because during the trial we had the opportunity of seeing that in one period, according to the testimonies of witnesses, your brother wore a beard. Did he wear it because of his affiliation to the Chetnik movement or was there another reason?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I also wore a beard when I was young for some time and then I shaved it. Dusko didn't wear a beard. He just wore a beard at one point in time. He was ill. Something was wrong, I think, on his right-hand side. He had some kind of tissue that started growing out there. This was very ugly to see. I told our mother: "Talk him into operating on that. I'll try to find a surgeon in Banja Luka so that he would handle that". She said he was afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Connected to this beard also we had heard that there was an exchange of personalities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I remember Mr. Wladimiroff was the first lawyer, and I was convinced that Dusko did not take part in any of this and I came to the conclusion and I will always say that, that he was replaced --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Tadic. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, we object to this line of questioning. It is attempting to traverse issues that were raised and dealt with at length in the trial. If it is any assistance to my friend, the Prosecution makes no issue about Mr. Tadic's character and the fact that he had a beard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Vujin, tell me where you are going with this line of testimony. I was concerned that there was statements that were going to be offered regarding Mr. Wladimiroff's involvement as prior counsel, and I thought that perhaps that was not necessary. That was really my concern, but tell me where you are going with this?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: The only direction that the Defence wishes to move into is to depict the possibility of Dusko Tadic before this court, because when you decide on the punishment, you have to know everything about his personality from his youth until these events and certainly the best information of this sort can be provided by his family and the people who knew him best. So we read all the statements carefully and we discussed this with our colleague, Mr. Wladimiroff, and there was no questioning of that sort, that is to show the personality of Dusko Tadic. So all of this is aimed at showing the personality of Dusko Tadic, his character, because we believe that this is very important for your decision, because we expect that decision to be passed by taking into consideration all the circumstances which are taken into account in all well-known legal systems. The level of culpability, criminal liability, according to our system is also important, and that level cannot be determined without fully looking into the personality and character of the person concerned, everything that can portray his character. So I don't think that the objection of the Prosecutor is well-founded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: What does the beard have to do with that? I think you have covered that, that he typically didn't wear a beard but wore one because of a growth on his neck. I think that is even in the report of the psychiatrist in Germany. I think you can move on to another area. I heard Mr. Tadic make the reference to --

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Absolutely. I will move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I heard Mr. Tadic make the reference to (redacted) as well as Sofjia Tadic. I hope you would confine the statement you elicit from Mr. Tadic to the character of the accused or the convicted person in this instance. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. We shall proceed and you can reject our questions, of course, and we will accept that. Do you know about the activities of your brother, Dusko Tadic, in the humanitarian field?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Can you explain these activities and what he did?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During the previous system as a boy he was a member of the youth organisation like all of us. He collected aid according to instructions received from adults, from the party organisation, and afterwards, as far as I know, during the conflicts. After the conflict in Kozarac, when Dusko came there to his home town, and after having worked in the Reserve Militia, then he worked in the Red Cross, Prijedor, too. He helped many people on many occasions especially to refugees, Serbs who came from Sasinska Krinanj who moved in there, but I must say that he particularly cared about a Croat family that came to stay right next door to us, the house of Salih Hantic. They are Croats. Dusko accommodated them there. He helped them. He brought them food every day. It was very difficult then and it was dangerous to help people of a different nationality, different ethnic background. Dusko didn't want to do them any harm. He wanted to help them. They are still living in Kozarac. They are leading a normal life. If somebody would come and ask about Dusko, ask them, you would see what they thought of Dusko.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: And, finally, Mr. Tadic, do you know whether any criminal proceedings are being carried out today against your brother in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I was in the command of the 5th Kozarac bringing aid in Omarska perhaps half a year ago or a year ago, and there is -- criminal proceedings were instituted against him then, because he didn't want to go to fight in the war. He didn't want to wear a uniform because not at a single point in time did Dusko want to wage war, did he want to go to the war. He thought it was a stupid, pointless war. It was the worst thing that could happen to people, and I think that he was afraid also, just like all of us. I tell you, I wasn't in the war but I was afraid whenever a grenade fell. There was not a single man who was not afraid. He was afraid of the war. He was terribly frightened of the war, and he said that as much as he could and in every way he could, he would try to avoid participating in the war, and that when he couldn't he would probably go as far away as possible and that is what he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tadic. I'm just interested in a few more things or rather one more thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I wonder if I can interrupt to ask you. I didn't understand that last piece of evidence. You asked about criminal proceedings being brought and I thought you were referring to criminal proceedings a year or so ago. That seemed to be the evidence. Is that what you are involved with?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Proceedings against Mr. Tadic instituted a year or so ago?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: The evidence did not clarify what they were, and before you leave the topic, you might clarify it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: I can try to clarify it with the witness. Thank you very much. You said that criminal proceedings were instituted because he ran away from his unit and because he didn't respond to the call that came from the military unit. Did you hear of Mile Cavic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think that was the commander of that unit and they wanted to mobilise Dusko into that unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Do you have any information as to how many times they came to call for your brother and how many times they came to bring him to that unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Several times in Prijedor and Banja Luka they looked for him and found him and brought him in twice, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: In the written submission we submitted today you have a statement by Mile Cavic, the commander of that company, concerning that event, and during this hearing we are going to give you all the court materials on that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Thank you. So none of this was a year or year and a half ago. It was some 3 or 4 years ago that the witness is speaking of; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: No. The event itself took place three or four years ago, specifically in 1993, but criminal proceedings were instituted in 1996, while they managed to gather all the data and they were looking for Dusko Tadic, and when they definitely realised that he went away, that he left the country. There are many such cases -- there were many such cases and the Prosecutor would initiate proceedings as sufficient information came in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tadic, did your brother drink alcohol or was he inclined to do so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No. He didn't drink at all. He would drink fruit juice and sometimes with a group of friends he would perhaps have a glass of wine, but these were exceptional situations, when we had parties with our friends. We would visit one another. So these would be exceptional occasions. Perhaps he would have a glass or two of wine, nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: And the final question, Mr. Tadic. Before these events and apart from the proceedings that we mentioned, did Dusko Tadic have any problems with the authorities and were any kind of proceedings ever instituted against him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean the previous authorities before these events?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Was he ever brought before a court of law or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No. I don't think that the authorities knew them. The commune was Prijedor and the local community was Kozarac. The authorities didn't really know him. He didn't make any kind of problem, because he went to school in Belgrade and then he went to school in Zagreb, the Applied Arts School. Our father couldn't afford to send all of us to school. There were four of us. He came back from Belgrade from school. Then he set up this karate club. Then he went to Ljubjana, Zagreb, Sisak, Belgrade. He had a private company, a firm of his own, and when he came back, yes, before our father died he came back, and then he opened a cafe. He earned some money and then also before they went to Libya and then a war broke out there. Then they had to go back. He really wanted to support his family, his two young children. If a person doesn't work, he can't survive, and it's very difficult to be the breadwinner, especially in our situation back there now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, to the best of your knowledge what was the relationship within the family of Dusko Tadic between him and his wife, etc?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very good.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, you confirmed in your evidence-in-chief that you came before this Chamber last year and gave evidence in the course of the trial. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: On that occasion you gave your evidence publicly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And, as I understand, there was no measures for protection or anything offered in favour of you on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: On this occasion are you aware of the fact that there has been an order made for your safe conduct to the Hague, that you won't be arrested while you are here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Has anything changed since the last occasion that you were here to make you want to make such a request?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably they have. That is why I made such a request.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Would you mind telling us what they are?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What has changed is that I know that Dusko Tadic did not participate in any sense in those conflicts. He has been in prison for three years and four months, and I know who fixed it, and I made my own investigation, and I am convinced that he has been substituted for somebody else, and if Dusko Tadic were to grow a beard for ten or fifteen days and have a haircut like that man, as that man did when Dusko Tadic was in the area of the Prijedor municipality, you would see that they were identical. If you took Dusko Tadic outside this courtroom, you wouldn't be able to recognise them one from the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I'm asking about yourself. What have you done to make you request a safe conduct order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I asked protection because I was a soldier in the army of Republika Srpska. If I know and I am 100 per cent sure that that man did nothing and this other man is driving the latest Mercedes and is enjoying luxury in life, then of course I will ask for protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I will interrupt you again. I'm asking what you have done. What have you personally done between last year and now to make you want to make this request for safe conduct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have been watching and listening to this trial, and I told Mr. Wladimiroff about this man, and you did nothing about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am not asking you about this other man. I am asking you about what you have done.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. Maybe I could be of some assistance. Have you received any threats in the meantime?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will probably have problems when I go back home, you see. That is what the situation is like over there. I have not received any threats from you personally, but for months I was called up at home. I was threatened, two women's voices and two men's voices. I had a recording. I gave that to Mr. Wladimiroff. I was threatened recently when Dusko was found guilty. These may be Serbs. They may be anyone. I don't know. But it is a fact that I have been placed in such a situation that I don't trust anyone any more. I have apologised, but I asked for protection so as to be sure that I could return to my family safely, because if I would have to prove my innocence like my brother has done, maybe I would suffer the same fate.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: I apologise. Maybe this is outside the subject matter of this pre-sentencing proceedings to talk about the character of the witness at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: The question was asked some time ago why the witness had asked for freedom from being arrested and whether he had done anything that would cause him to fear that he would be arrested and, as I understand your answer, it is that you have not done anything -- correct me if I am wrong -- but you have received threats, and you did not know what might happen to you if you came to the Hague. I have omitted a lot. That's for sure.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Threats, you mean? I just told you that I was threatened on the phone several times, so I asked for protection simply.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Just confining yourself to that specific issue, the threats that you received on the phone, are you suggesting that that came from somebody in the Tribunal. Is that what you are suggesting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So you are not suggesting that you are fearful of anyone in the Tribunal causing you any harm or difficulty while you are in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Vujin, do you have additional questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: We have no questions. Thank you, Mr. Tadic, for coming again to the Tribunal. You are now excused.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: We will stand in recess until 4 o'clock. Hopefully your other witnesses will be here by then, Mr. Vujin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. There was a matter that I was wondering if I might raise at the moment. There is a name mentioned in the testimony which I have written on this piece of yellow paper, which I would ask to be shown to the Defence and your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: You wish a redaction?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I understand I am too late, your Honour, for the redaction. It will appear in the transcript unless your Honours make an order to the contrary. It appears at page 19, line 16. I simply ask that that name be redacted from the transcript. It was a witness, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I know that it was mentioned twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I will find out the reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Both references.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Both references I would ask to be redacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Is there any objection, Mr. Vujin?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: We understand the submission of the Prosecutor, but I was saying at the beginning in connection with other persons it is very difficult to ask the witness: "Who is so and so?" You know that was a problem we had at the beginning. I believe that there is no reason to have this name redacted from the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think I will have to go into closed session or into private session if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I remember the witness. The witness was not a protected witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, that's right, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Why don't we do that at the close. Is Mr. Ljubomir -- I understand he is to be recalled. Is he available now? Can we hear Mr. Ljubomir and another witness and then do this at the end, since we do not have enough time to redact it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Mr. Ljubomir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Is this witness being recalled?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Yes. I was advised that Mr. Ljubomir Tadic is to be recalled. Do you have any objection, Mr. Niemann? I had assumed you had been told of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I have heard of it but I was not aware whether he was to be recalled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: We will hear further from Mr. Tadic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Ljubomir Tadic (recalled).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, you had been excused. I thought that your testimony -- you had completed your testimony. You had previously taken an oath to tell the truth. I will ask that you confirm that you still accept that oath and the testimony that you will be giving will be under oath, the same oath that you took before. Do you agree to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Vujin?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: After the examination, during the break, we came to the conclusion that we have not fully clarified the circumstances recording a part of your testimony when you said, and I think that is quite clear, that your brother has been persecuted by the bodies of the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: We would like to clarify a little the circumstances that led up to this persecution, aside from his failing to respond to the call-up. You are aware that upon the issuance of the mobilisation he tried and managed to be engaged as a reserve traffic policeman. Did you participate in this? In what way? Will you explain please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time Dusko was with me. Rather, he was in Banja Luka. He spent most of his time in my house. The house that he was staying in is not far from my flat, where I live. He used my telephone and on several occasions I tried to get in touch with Mr. Dusan Jankovic, Deputy Chief of the Interior in Prijedor. He is a close family friend, and I tried to intervene so that he may join up with the traffic, reserve traffic police and avoid the military call-up. We got into touch. I said traffic policeman, yes. We got in touch and we also called Radovan Vokic, who was an active policeman, and Dusan Jankovic was chief of the traffic police, and that is why we called him, and he promised to admit Dusko as a member of the reserve traffic police. As I said when I was here the last time, the general mobilisation was on 16th June 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, after all that, when your brother was arrested and virtually kidnapped, did you know where he was? Was the family aware of his whereabouts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew he was having problems, since he was working in Kozarac in the local commune.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask that my friend use terminology other than "kidnapped" or if he wants to use that terminology, to explain in what context he uses it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I will overrule your objection. You may proceed, Mr. Vujin.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. For my learned friend to hear and understand why we use this term, it is because our client, Mr. Dusko Tadic, was taken away in a manner that corresponds to the term used, and that is why I use the term. Therefore, Mr. Ljubomir Tadic, were you aware where your brother was? Did you look for him? How did you look for him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I looked for him. I reacted immediately when I learned what had happened. I called Prijedor several times. Nobody wanted to answer. Then I went there myself. I found a couple of people. Nobody knew anything or didn't want to say anything. I came across the former President of SDS in Prijedor, Simo Miskovic. I asked him and he said: "I know nothing but I'll try to find out ". Then I learned that he was in Gradacac. I assumed that was where he could be, because that unit was in Gradacac. Through a colleague of mine, a lawyer in the company, Ludi Jariz, that I worked in, he was also with a unit there. Then I asked him to go and check and find out where my brother is. He was arrested and taken away and I don't know what happened to him. It was very difficult. For a moment I thought he had even been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Did he manage to get away?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He got away, but then he was arrested once again and taken to the front. Afterwards he didn't want to go anywhere. I know exactly the policeman who arrested him. I think his name was Desimir. After his arrest in Germany I found Desimir and he said at one point that he would testify to that effect, but he was probably not allowed to.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Who didn't permit him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The people in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: After July 1st, 1993, when he left the unit for the last time, was he in hiding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He hid in my apartment until he left for Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: And from Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And from Belgrade to Germany and then I learned through the media that he had been arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Do you know -- you probably do -- that he had problems with his apartment in Prijedor, that he was evicted from his flat? Can you tell us anything about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He was given an apartment for temporary use in Pecani. He was there with his family for a time. When these arrests occurred, as he didn't have permanent tenancy over this flat, he was evicted, and I think a colleague of his wife gave them a small apartment as you enter Prijedor, a building on the left-hand side with four or five stories -- there's a bank downstairs -- and he used this flat temporarily. I know he didn't dare to go and pick up his things so he asked me to do it. I found a colleague. I gave him 50 Deutschemarks for the fuel to take his truck, and I went to him and my oldest son Nenad; a man called Slobodan, the owner of this truck; Saca Maric, a young man who was on leave at the time, a man from Banja Luka, who knew Dusko well, and before Dusko's departure I think they kept company in Banja Luka. We went to Prijedor and very quickly secretly we collected his things -- there were very few -- because he didn't dare go himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Did your brother ever get anything from the state authorities in the sense of an apartment or any other property or anything in the sense of a reward?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Let us go back to the causes of the persecution. Do you know that before the conflict broke out in Kozarac were there any attempts to clear up certain things that occurred as a dispute between the municipality and the citizens of Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I know quite a bit about those events and I can provide documents as evidence. Quite recently I was looking for some documents and I found a document. I can give it to you tomorrow. When I was in Kozarac I said that I had a beer discount store, and I have a document when that beer was being delivered on the 21st for the last time. So I spent quite a bit of time there. I know what was happening. I know that Dusko was a member of the civic forum.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Now what is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it's a kind of a non-party organisation, an organisation which rallied Serbs, Muslims and all others, people who -- I knew who led this organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: At whose request did he join?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the request of Kemal Susic, a teacher of physical education and a neighbour of ours, who actually formed this civil alliance, and I was present when he asked Dusko to join him so that they should form a delegation and go to Prijedor. The atmosphere was highly tense at the time and everybody was afraid, including Dusko, and of course the Muslims in Kozarac, too, that a conflict could break out. There were lots of people, as anywhere else. I do not claim that only the Muslims were extremists. There were extremists on all sides, the Serbs, the Muslims and Croats. In Kozarac that were extremists from among the members of the SDA that would not allow this civil forum to function. There were many provocations. I remember Kemal Susic took his pupils and led them along the Main Street of Kozarac bearing placards. They were all there together.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Did your brother participate in those talks with representatives of the Prijedor municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I was there. There was Dusko -- maybe I won't remember all the names -- there was Dusko, Kemal Susic, Hamdija Kahrimanovic -- I think he was the school principal at the time -- Fazic. He was director of the sawmill.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Do you consider this to have been one of the reasons --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Excuse me. You have an objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. I don't know why we are traversing all of this evidence which we went through at great length at trial. I don't see how anyway it assists your Honour in assessing the character of Mr. Tadic, so I object to it, because I don't see where it is leading us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Vujin, we did hear testimony about Mr. Tadic's involvement with the group of Muslims and Serbs, as I recall, meeting with mostly Muslims, and Mr. Tadic was representative because he was Serb, meeting with authorities in Prijedor. We heard a lot of testimony about that and we heard regarding Kemal Susic. We don't need to hear about Mr. Kemal Susic, that's for sure. So I think as far as his involvement and Mr. Tadic's involvement in this effort, we've heard it. If you want to highlight something, then you may.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Yes. We don't insist on the name of these witnesses. We are just trying to convey to you, as the Trial Chamber, the facts which will serve as a basis for you to be able to draw conclusions on the character of Dusko Tadic as well as the fact that he was persecuted by Republika Srpska, and this persecution started when he joined this Civil Forum and when he refused to be mobilised, and he sought connections and friends to join the reserve traffic police, refusing to bear arms and wear a uniform, and we feel this is important for his characterisation. One further question for Mr. Tadic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: As long as we are focussing on his character and not the character of witnesses who have come to testify, because this may be kind of a way to challenge the evidence that has already been received and accepted, and it has happened twice. I'm afraid that we are now getting close to a third incident. If that's not where you are going, fine, but we are aware of this. So one further question on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, do you believe that your brother, Dusko Tadic, could return safely to the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wouldn't advise it since the people in power, who came into power in 1992 are still in power. The same people are in power, so I would not advise him to go back.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Do you feel that he would be persecuted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He wouldn't be safe and his very life may be in danger.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann? Just one question, Mr. Tadic. You testified a few moments ago about your calling in an effort to obtain a position for Mr. Tadic as a traffic policeman. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: You mentioned a number of names of people whom you called. Did you also call Mr. Vokic? Do you remember your testimony when you were here and you testified you called Mr. Vokic and he is related, a distant relative?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Radovan Vokic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: You did?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Radovan Vokic among others. He was already an active policeman, traffic policeman. He was already employed full-time, so he could help to persuade our friend to admit Dusko as a reserve traffic policeman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Vujin, do you have additional questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: None. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, you are excused once again. Thank you very much for coming. I think you are permanently excused. Mr. Vujin, would you call your next witness, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Witness sworn

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Vujin, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam, you are a friend of the Tadic family. You and your husband were friends with some of the Tadic family members?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: With whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Do you know the family circumstances involved?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: What was the life of the Tadic family like and where did they live?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They lived in Kozarac and they lived the life of an ordinary family.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Who lived in their family home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dusko and his family, the mother and the father.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Are his parents still alive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The father died. The mother is still alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Do you know what the mother's health is like now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She's very ill.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: So you were friends practically?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With the family of Dusko Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Do you know the other brothers of Dusko Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I know them very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Did you meet them also?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Where usually?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: In which situations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Usually on 1st May, when they slaughtered animals, also sometimes for the New Year.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: You mentioned the slaughter of animals. You mean pigs, swine, as customary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Did Dusko Tadic take part in these rituals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he usually did housework.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Did he avoid that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because he couldn't stand the sight of blood. He couldn't stand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Could you tell us when would you see each other, would Dusko drink alcoholic beverages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, very rarely, only wine, a glass or two.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Did you ever see him drunk?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Would you say whether Dusko was inclined to quarrel, fight?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No. He was a very good man and a good friend.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: What does that mean, being a good friend, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I consider him to be a good friend and I (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted).

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Tell me when you would see each other and sit together, did you talk about every day matters, for example whether somebody had a hobby or whether he had a hobby?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Do you know whether Dusko had a hobby?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: What?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was fond of painting.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Could you tell me how come you know? What did you receive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is because I had a painting made by him in my apartment. It's a present.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: He gave it to you as a present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: So you would sit together and talk?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: If you don't mind, can I ask you what are you by nationality in terms of ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Your husband?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He is a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: When you would sit together and talk, did Dusko Tadic or any member of his family ever bring up that question of Croats or Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Did they divide people according to ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we also had Muslim friends too.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Do you know what their relationship was with their neighbours and whether they had Muslims who were neighbours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and they had very good relationships with them. I know very well the next-door-neighbour of Dusko Tadic. Kiba was her name.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: And the relations were very good?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very good.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Do you know about Dusko Tadic's activity in the sports field?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: What was he involved in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that he trained karate. I don't know if I'm using the right terminology.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Do you know anything more about that, whether he was a coach? Who did he coach?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Young people.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: And these young people, of what ethnic background were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most of them Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: After being friends with Dusko Tadic and before these actual events in the territory of Opstina Prijedor took place, did you know anything about the political activities of Dusko Tadic and whether he had any?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Do you know that Dusko was persecuted by the authorities of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time he stayed with me. I knew that something was happening but I didn't know about anything in detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Did you know that he was evicted from his apartment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I know that but I don't know how and why.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that Dusko was arrested and brought in by the military police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't really tell you exactly. I can't respond to that exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Can you explain to us -- I'll show you a photograph here, with your permission. I just want to ask you whether you can recognise what you see in this photograph. (Handed)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This is Dusko Tadic's house in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: So that is the apartment of Dusko Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: On the right-hand side on the wall there is a tapestry. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Can you describe it to us because we cannot see in the photograph here what it actually depicts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is the portrait of Comrade Tito.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: The family of Dusko Tadic, was it brought up in that spirit, in the partisan spirit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: His father, although he was a partisan, did he enjoy a high reputation in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Did you attend his father's funeral?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Can you describe that funeral to me in the sense of the number of people who attended and who bathed the father ritually?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My husband was the one who bathed his father's body and there were very many people. It was a huge funeral. I think I had never seen such a big funeral.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Who was present, citizens of what ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Everybody from Kozarac was there. Everybody was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Do you know the extent to which his cafe was damaged?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: How did it happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I couldn't explain that to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Was your house damaged?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Do you know how?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know. A grenade was shot at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Who shot?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Finally, what could you say about Dusko, a person who you were friends with? What kind of a person is he? What kind of character?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He's a very good friend, careful, generous.
